thread.title: 231 Billion Reasons Apple Should Spin Off Its Services Business

author: admin
title: 231 Billion Reasons Apple Should Spin Off Its Services Business
text:
231 Billion Reasons Apple Should Spin Off Its Services Business
&l;p&g;&l;img class=&q;dam-image getty size-large wp-image-477483948&q; src=&q;https://specials-images.forbesimg.com/dam/imageserve/477483948/960×0.jpg?fit=scale&q; data-height=&q;640&q; data-width=&q;960&q;&g; NEW YORK, NY – JUNE 17: The Apple logo is displayed at the Apple Store June 17, 2015 on Fifth Avenue in New York City. Photo by Eric Thayer/Getty Images
Apple&s;s biggest business — accounting for some 60% of its revenues — is the 11 year old iPhone. But that mature business is barely growing. Fortunately for investors, Apple has a smaller business that&s;s growing faster — its so-called Services unit which includes revenues from App Store downloads, iCloud storage and Apple Music subscriptions.
If Services — which enjoyed a 31% pop to over $9 billion in the first quarter of 2018 — was a separately-traded company, it would command a much higher valuation than Apple — which has been growing at a &l;a href=&q;http://www.morningstar.com/stocks/xnas/aapl/quote.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;five year average rate of 7.9%&l;/a&g;.
Should Apple spin off&a;nbsp;Services? By keeping Services inside the company, Apple is&a;nbsp;holding back&a;nbsp;$231 billion in value from shareholders. (I have no financial interest in Apple securities).
Before getting into that, a well-known strategic error is for a company to depend too heavily on a single product.&a;nbsp;After all,&a;nbsp;if that product is popular and represents a&a;nbsp;big opportunity, it will attract competitors who may take market share from the incumbent by offering a lower-priced version that many consumers find irresistible.
The remedy for this error is innovation — but not all CEOs can do it well. Some, like&a;nbsp;Steve Jobs,&a;nbsp;are able to build on a company&s;s strengths to create much better products aimed at&a;nbsp;large markets. Jobs was able to accomplish this with amazing success in the MP3 Player, cell phone, and tablet markets.
His successor, Tim Cook, has tried — for example, he oversaw the launch of the Apple&a;nbsp;Watch. But that product&a;nbsp;does not&a;nbsp;generate enough revenue to make much of a difference.
How so? Bundled in Other&a;nbsp;for&a;nbsp;financial reporting purposes&a;nbsp;with AirPods, Apple TV, Beats products, iPod Touch and the HomePod, the Apple Watch was an unspecified part of Other&s;s $5.5 billion, or 6.2% of Apple&s;s first quarter 2018 revenue of &l;a href=&q;https://techcrunch.com/2018/02/01/apple-5-5-billion-revenue-other-products-q1-2018/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;$88.3 billion&l;/a&g;.
Along with the iPhone, Jobs oversaw the introduction of the App Store and&a;nbsp;iTunes which&a;nbsp;made the profitable devices Apple sold much more compelling to consumers.
Under Jobs, Apple did not make much profit on these services but they fueled demand for&a;nbsp;its highly profitable hardware — for example, in&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://www.forbes.com/sites/petercohan/2013/01/30/why-wall-street-loves-amazon-not-apple/#26655ab64f56&q; target=&q;_self&q;&g;September 2012&l;/a&g;&a;nbsp;due to its 44% higher price and lower&a;nbsp;unit cost, Apple earned a whopping 71% gross margin on its iPhone 4S&a;nbsp;&l;span&g;– much higher than the Nokia Lumina&s;s &l;/span&g;54% gross margin.
But in recent years, iPhone revenues have not been growing rapidly and predictably. To wit,&a;nbsp;they increased 3% in 2017, fell 12% in 2016, and soared 52% in 2015.
To his credit, Cook presided over the decision to report to investors the financial results of its Services unit.&a;nbsp; And according to Gene Munster of&a;nbsp;&l;a href=&q;http://loupventures.com/apple-services-tracking-to-20-of-revenue-in-five-years/&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Loup Ventures,&l;/a&g; Services has grown at an average annual rate of 22% since 2006.
According to the &l;a href=&q;https://www.ft.com/content/b5f66f16-5f61-11e8-9334-2218e7146b04&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;em&g;Financial Times,&l;/em&g;&l;/a&g; Munster used a price/sales ratio of 10 — by looking at software as a service companies like Adobe, Dropbox or Intuit — to estimate that Services would enjoy a market capitalization of $381 billion — assuming it will generate $38.1 billion in 2018 revenue (Cook&s;s 2020 target is $50 billion) — if it was a standalone company.
Applying Apple&s;s price/sales ratio of &l;a href=&q;https://blogs.forbes.com/petercohan/wp-admin/post.php?post=31931&a;amp;action=edit&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;3.93&l;/a&g; to that 2018 estimate — which would value the services revenue at $150 billion — suggests that Cook is&a;nbsp;holding back&a;nbsp;a whopping $231 billion in shareholder value from Apple investors.
The potential of Services is based on a growing number of Apple devices owners and a rise in the service revenue per device. In January 2016,&a;nbsp;Apple disclosed that it had&a;nbsp;more than 1 billion active iOS devices — smartphones, tablets, watches and its TV set-top boxes — to which it could sell services, according to the Financial Times.
Over the last four years, that number has grown about 30%&a;nbsp;to 1.3 billion during which time services revenues doubled.
Morgan Stanley&s;s Katy Huberty noted that Apple&s;s paid subscriptions — from its own services, including Music, as well as third-party apps like Netflix or Spotify — grew from 100 million in 2017 to 270 million this year.
Of course, when it comes to services, Apple faces plenty of competition from standalone services suppliers and from its current partners. Bernstein Research&s;s Toni Sacconaghi&a;nbsp;estimated that&a;nbsp;Google paid Apple as much as $5 billion in the last year to&a;nbsp;maintain its position as&a;nbsp;the iPhone&a;rsquo;s default search engine.
According to the Financial times, as Sacconaghi wrote in a client note
&l;/p&g;&l;blockquote&g;Google&a;rsquo;s willingness to share material revenues with Apple is a testament to the power of Apple&a;rsquo;s iOS platform, but we see it as a double-edged sword. While it&a;rsquo;s hard to say if Google might ever stop paying Apple &a;hellip; it certainly represents a potential risk.&l;/blockquote&g;
Since Apple does not report on the profitability of its Services unit, investors are left to wonder whether it is adding to Apple&s;s overall profitability. But signs suggest that the investment required to keep up with competitors might be bringing Services overall profitability below Apple&s;s corporate gross margin of 38.3%, according to &l;a href=&q;https://www.reuters.com/article/us-apple-services/apple-services-segment-faces-margin-competitive-challenges-idUSKBN1I32KX&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;&l;em&g;Reuters&l;/em&g;&l;/a&g;.
Two Services businesses are likely high margin. The 10 year old&a;nbsp; App Store receives 30% of the price of one-time and in-app purchases and 15% of App&a;nbsp;Store subscriptions to&a;nbsp;&a;nbsp;services like Netflix after a year. Apple&a;rsquo;s iCloud online storage business enjoyed a 50%&a;nbsp;revenue pop in the first Reuters,&a;nbsp;and its gross margin is likely closer to Dropbox&s;s 68%.
Apple Music — which competes with money losers like &l;a href=&q;http://www.morningstar.com/stocks/xnys/spot/quote.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Spotify Technology&l;/a&g; and &l;a href=&q;http://www.morningstar.com/stocks/xnys/p/quote.html&q; target=&q;_blank&q;&g;Pandora Media&l;/a&g;— and Apple&s;s video business — where Apple plans to spend $1 billion developing original video content — are probably not so profitable.
In addition to potentially unlocking hundreds of billions in shareholder value, spinning off&a;nbsp;Apple Services would take away all the mystery surrounding its growth potential and profitability.
